newsitem.title: BELGIUM: New report slams Nigerian human rights record.
newsitem.headline: New report slams Nigerian human rights record.

text.p: A major human rights report to be released on Friday chronicles a catalogue of alleged murder, torture and sustained oppression in Nigeria and calls on the international community to isolate the West African country.
The 52-page report, compiled by Human Rights Watch, accuses the military government headed by General Sani Abacha of having no intention of ever relinquishing power.
Human Rights Watch is an international non-governmental organisation founded in 1978 to press for and monitor internationally accepted standards of free society.
The report, released in Belgium, the United States, the Netherlands and Britain, says international outrage at human rights abuses has been dulled by economic considerations.
It warns that a failure to press for change will entrench the government and lead to further abuse.
A spokesman for the Nigerian embassy in Brussels said he was not aware of the report and reserved comment until after he had seen it.
Abacha's government, which seized power in 1993, has been repeatedly criticised by the United Nations, Organisation of African Unity, the Commonwealth and the European Union for human rights abuse.

Abacha nullified elections -- held to choose a civilian government to replace years of military rule by General Ibrahim Babangida -- and jailed Chief Mahsood Abiola, who was popularly believed to have been the winner.

International outrage at Abacha's government reached a high point last November following the execution of author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other members of the Movement for Survival of Ogoni Peoples who had been convicted by a military-appointed court of the murder of four Ogoni chiefs.

In New York on Thursday, Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy accused some fellow Commonwealth members of being "appeasers", saying they were allowing the Nigerian government "to get away with" executing Saro-Wiwa.
The Human Rights Watch report says hundreds of opposition activists arrested under the guise of a "crime crackdown" are being held without trial throughout the country.
It says that nearly half of 45,000 people in Nigeria's jails are awaiting trial and conditions are so bad that over 4,000 prisoners die in custody each year.

It names dozens of people -- including children -- it says have been tortured by Nigerian authorities and lists examples of forced resettlement, evictions and expulsions the government is carrying out to quash opposition.
The report is also critical of the Royal Dutch Petroleum Company, which controls the Shell Group, for not doing more to pressure the Nigerian government into change.
Shell, which is responsible for the production of about 40 percent of Nigeria's oil extracts, has faced a consumer boycott in recent years because of its links to Nigeria.
A Shell spokesman in London declined to comment on the report until management had had time to study it.
